## Final visualization

```{r}
#| label: final-setup
#| include: false
# prepares the explorer using the models fitted in the previous section
source("R/final/setup.R")

percent <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
latest <- max(model_years)
observed_rule <- joint |>
    filter(test == "national", test_year == latest) |>
    summarise(any = sum(share[gap > 0]), full = sum(share[gap >= 1]))

by_advice <- national_explorer$decomposition |>
    filter(test_year == latest, test == "national average")
design_for <- function(advice) {
    percent(by_advice$category_design[by_advice$advice == advice])
}
```

The same results answer different questions for different readers.
Policy makers set the rules of the advice, school boards choose the test for their schools,
and parents want to know what the test means for their child at a particular school.
Therefore, our final visualization is an explorer (@fig-explorer) that shows the decomposition of @sec-decomposition
for different granularities:
the Netherlands, every province, municipality, school board, group of schools with a similar school weighting, and single school.
It answers three questions:

- Where does the eligibility for a higher track come from, and who can change each source?
- How would the eligibility change with another test or, for a single school, with the teachers of another school?
- What can the test change for a child with a given provisional advice at that school?

School boards can check whether the test of their schools suits their pupils, and whether their teachers advise in line with the test.
Parents can see whether a school tends to advise lower than the test results suggest, and how much a more lenient test would help their child.
For the Netherlands, the explorer shows the national model for 2025 and 2026.
For groups of schools and single schools, it uses a school-level version of the model for 2025,
the only year with both school data and a fitted model.


### Eligibility explorer {#sec-final-explorer}

```{r}
#| label: fig-explorer
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Eligibility explorer. Search the Netherlands, a province, municipality, school board, group of similar schools, or school, and choose the pupils (all, or those with one provisional advice) and what-ifs above the figure. Top: where eligibility for a higher track comes from (hover over the info icons for what each source means and who can change it); the diamond marks the observed share of pupils with a higher test advice. Bottom: the test results of these pupils, one icon per percent. Sources: model fitted to CvTE [@cvte2025; @cvte2026] with Cito's resit share [@cito2026]; school data from DUO [@duo_heroverweging; @duo_advies; @duo_eindscores; @duo_schooladviezen; @duo_adressen] and the Inspectorate [@inspectie_schoolweging]."  # nolint: line_length_linter
eligibility_explorer(
    school_estimates, national_explorer, gap_matrix, compliance
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal" title="Data table"}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-explorer-national
#| tbl-cap: "National decomposition of eligibility in the latest year, among all pupils and per provisional advice."  # nolint: line_length_linter
by_advice |>
    select(-test_year, -test) |>
    knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```
:::

The waterfall in @fig-explorer shows the model's decomposition of eligibility (@eq-decomposition).
Where available, a diamond marks the observed share for comparison.
Search and navigation links switch between schools and groups; what-ifs recompute the model with another test or another school's estimated teacher leniency.
The vertical line marks the estimate without that change. Note that these are model scenarios.

In the national CvTE tables for `{r} latest`, `{r} percent(observed_rule$any)` of pupils have a higher test advice, but only `{r} percent(observed_rule$full)` have a difference of at least a full level.
The model's error-free reference scenario estimates eligibility of `{r} design_for("havo")` among pupils assigned havo advice in that scenario; this is not an observed share attributable to category design.

The 100 dots show rounded outcome proportions for the selected group and advice.
National dots use observed CvTE tables; when a test is selected, they describe its actual participants, while the waterfall models that test for the national population.
School and group dots use model estimates.

School estimates depend on the model assumptions and limited pupil counts.
The stricter/more-lenient label uses an estimated leniency at least two standard errors from zero; the warning below 20 pupils is an additional caution.
